solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Favoured puritan concealing repulsive ends occasionally

indicators.note: the puritan word hides the next piece within it, so it wraps around it

parts.note: a prig is a self-righteously prim person, a puritan
vile means repulsive

indicators.note: taking letters only now and then from the word ends, i.e. every other one

explanation.surface: A favoured but strait-laced person secretly harbours some unpleasant aims now and again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concealing' wraps the puritan around the repulsive word; 'occasionally' picks the first and third letters of 'ends'.
explanation.definitionFit: Privileged people enjoy special advantages, so they are favoured ones.

clue.text: Reportedly travelled zigzag courses — imposition on driver?

indicators.note: signals that the phrase is to be heard spoken rather than read as written

parts.note: rode tacks: a sailor tacking zigzags against the wind

explanation.surface: A sailor's zigzagging voyage is linked, somehow, to a charge levied on motorists.
explanation.walkthrough: To tack is to sail a zigzag course into the wind, so 'travelled zigzag courses' is RODE TACKS, which spoken sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Road tax is the duty a motorist must pay to use a vehicle, a levy imposed on drivers.

clue.text: Holiday home in very rough area

parts.note: feeling rough means feeling ill

explanation.surface: A holiday home is found in a very rough neighbourhood.
explanation.definitionFit: A villa is a house rented or owned for vacations, typically abroad in the sun.

clue.text: Circuit record where one takes first place in concise style

parts.note: a lap is one circuit of a track

indicators.note: the numeral for one is moved up to the front of the record word

parts.note: a diary is a daily record
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A lap record is set, with someone winning the race, in a pithy account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'where one takes first place' moves the record's I to its front, giving IDARY.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapidary describes elegant, terse prose suited to inscriptions carved in stone.

clue.text: 8 20 has tough target after beating Spain

indicators.note: the Spain letter comes after the scrambled words
a beaten mixture is stirred up, so these words are scrambled

parts.note: E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: The England boss faces a hard objective after defeating Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beating' shuffles HAS TOUGH TARGET; 'after' puts E (Spain) at the end. 8 20 reads as ENGLAND MANAGER, the cross-referenced answers.
explanation.definitionFit: Gareth Southgate was the manager of the England men's football team from 2016 to 2024.

clue.text: Lives comfortably in Dumfries's outskirts

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
the outskirts of the town name are its outermost letters, first and last

parts.note: living well is living comfortably

explanation.surface: Someone lives in comfort on the edge of the Scottish town of Dumfries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts WELL between D and S, the outskirts of Dumfries's.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwell somewhere is to reside or make one's home there.

clue.text: Motley Crue ultimately in decline — it's over

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step
over in a down-and-back sense: the word for decline is turned round

parts.note: a dip is a decline

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the band's name

explanation.surface: The rock band Motley Crue is finally in decline; it's all finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's over' turns DIP into PID, and 'in' puts E, the last of Crue, inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Pied means of mixed colours, as of a magpie or a jester's motley costume.

clue.text: American region: area thrice opting out

indicators.note: out as in out of order: the letters are rearranged

parts.note: A for area, three times over

explanation.surface: A US region votes three times to leave something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' shuffles AAA with OPTING.
explanation.definitionFit: Patagonia is the southern tip of South America, a region of the Americas.

clue.text: Glenda Jackson finally restored country

indicators.note: restored as in rebuilt or reassembled, so the letters are rearranged
finally points to the closing letter of the surname

explanation.surface: The actress-turned-politician Glenda Jackson finally brought her nation back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' gives N from Jackson; 'restored' shuffles it with GLENDA.
explanation.definitionFit: England is a nation forming part of the United Kingdom.

clue.text: Pass from 8's number 7 in 1966

definitions.meaning: in football a ... is a pass to a teammate, as in 'a great ...'
Alan ... wore number 7 for England when they won the 1966 World Cup

explanation.surface: A pass from England's number 7 in the 1966 World Cup final.
explanation.definitionFit: A footballer's ball is a pass, and Alan Ball was England's 1966 midfielder.

clue.text: Say at exhibition centre salesperson returned profit

indicators.note: returned means the whole string is read back to front

parts.note: e.g. means for example, or say
the NEC is the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham
a rep is a sales representative

explanation.surface: At a trade show, a salesman got back his cut of the profits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' reverses the whole string. The NEC is a large exhibition venue near Birmingham.
explanation.definitionFit: A percentage is a cut or share of the takings, i.e. a profit.

clue.text: London thoroughfare: bear right to make entry

indicators.note: the right letter goes in, entering the word for bear

parts.note: to stand something is to bear it

explanation.surface: On a London street, keep right to get in.
explanation.walkthrough: The Strand is a major street in central London, running from Trafalgar Square to Fleet Street.
explanation.definitionFit: The Strand is a famous main road in the West End of London.

clue.text: Message from Mrs Simpson allowed to be read back

indicators.note: the words are read from end to start

parts.note: Marge Simpson is Homer's wife in The Simpsons
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A note from Mrs Simpson may be read aloud again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be read back' reverses MARGE LET.
explanation.definitionFit: A telegram is a message sent by telegraph and delivered on paper.

clue.text: Looks around old place adjoining extremely deficient forest?

parts.note: ex- means former or old
PL is the abbreviation for place in addresses

indicators.note: the word lacks its extremes, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone surveys an old site next to a sparse woodland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely deficient' trims forest to ORES.
explanation.definitionFit: To explore is to look around somewhere new to discover it.

clue.text: Laird wants hill encircled by road and river

indicators.note: the hill word sits inside the road word

parts.note: a lane is a minor road
a down is a rolling hill, as in the South Downs

explanation.surface: A Scottish estate owner wants a hill ringed by a road and a river.
explanation.walkthrough: A laird is a Scottish landed proprietor; 'encircled by' sets the hill inside the road. Downs are rolling chalk hills in southern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird is a Scottish owner of a large estate, so a landowner.

clue.text: Be jogger? It's no good without kit

indicators.note: the letter for good is missing, taken out

parts.note: to nudge someone is to jog them, so being a jogger is nudging

explanation.surface: A runner is told it's no use exercising without proper sports gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be jogger' looks like an invitation to run; it means to jog someone's elbow, NUDGE, which loses its G.
explanation.definitionFit: Nude means naked, wearing no clothes or kit at all.

clue.text: So doctor about to crack clue: the last

indicators.note: the reversed pair splits open the clue word

parts.note: a hint is a clue

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the pair is reversed

parts.note: MD is a Doctor of Medicine

explanation.surface: A puzzler's doctor is about to solve the final clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' gives DMOS, which 'to crack' places inside the clue word. 'about to crack' reads as 'nearly solving'; split it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hindmost means furthest behind, the one at the very back.

clue.text: Port served in a speakeasy?

parts.note: a speakeasy was an illicit drinking den during Prohibition

explanation.surface: Port wine is poured in an illegal bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' looks like the drink served; it is the Yemeni harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: Aden is a seaport in Yemen on the Gulf of Aden.

clue.text: Row D is located above E

indicators.note: in a down clue, above means placed before

parts.note: to put something somewhere is to locate it

explanation.surface: A seating row labelled D is found over row E.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' reads as a line of seats; it is a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: A row (rhyming with cow) is a quarrel or argument, i.e. a dispute.

clue.text: On warpath in uniform, spike the guns

parts.note: U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a pin is a spike
arms are weapons, guns

explanation.surface: A soldier on the warpath, in uniform, spikes the enemy's cannon.
explanation.walkthrough: To spike a gun was to disable it by driving a spike into its touch-hole.
explanation.definitionFit: Being up in arms means being angry and ready to fight.

clue.text: Staff argue regularly and run for supervisor

parts.note: to man something is to staff it

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of argue

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Employees routinely quarrel and dash off to their boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes AGE from argue.
explanation.definitionFit: A manager oversees staff and their work, so a supervisor.

clue.text: Essential elements in six stories English banned

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals

indicators.note: the English letter is barred, taken out of the stories word

parts.note: tales are stories

explanation.surface: Key parts of six tales have been banned in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banned' removes E from TALES.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitals are the body's vital organs, its essential parts.

clue.text: Surprise greatly — like 3?

definitions.meaning: 3 is VILLA; something like Aston Villa might jokingly be called ...

explanation.surface: Something greatly amazing is compared to a holiday home.
explanation.walkthrough: Aston Villa is a Birmingham football club; adding -ish (somewhat like) to Aston gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To astonish is to amaze or astound someone.

clue.text: Audacious in drag when dancing

indicators.note: dancing letters move about, so the words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Bold in women's clothing while dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when dancing' shuffles IN DRAG.
explanation.definitionFit: Daring means bold and willing to take risks, i.e. audacious.

clue.text: Security provider with stock to plunder

definitions.meaning: a gun, giving protection, with a wooden stock

explanation.surface: A security firm with goods in store sets out to loot.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifle is a stocked firearm, and to rifle a place is to search and steal from it.

clue.text: Bat droppings all around hit American in Cuban city

indicators.note: the droppings word goes all the way round the rest

parts.note: guano is the droppings of bats or seabirds
to tan someone is to beat them

explanation.surface: Bat mess surrounding an American who was struck in a Cuban city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all around' puts the droppings around the beating and the American.
explanation.definitionFit: Guantánamo is a city in south-eastern Cuba, beside the US naval base.

clue.text: Fuddy-duddy vaguely remembered losing a grand

indicators.note: losing means one letter goes missing

parts.note: a foggy memory is a vague one
G stands for a grand, a thousand pounds or dollars

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned person half-recalls losing a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' takes one G out of FOGGY.
explanation.definitionFit: A fogy (or fogey) is an old-fashioned, stuffy person.

clue.text: British always getting pint

parts.note: e'er is the poetic contraction of ever, always

explanation.surface: Britons are always having a pint.
explanation.definitionFit: A pint is the standard British serving of beer in a pub.

clue.text: Stormy weather set for ducks?

definitions.note: ducks is a British term of endearment, used to a single person, as is the answer

indicators.note: stormy means turbulent, so the letters are tossed about

explanation.surface: Bad weather is ideal for ducks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stormy' shuffles WEATHER SET. 'Ducks' seems to be the birds; in northern England it is a fond way to address someone, like 'love'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are affectionate forms of address for a loved one.
